---
title: "Performance and caching"
---

A prediction takes milliseconds. Reaching the first one takes seconds, because the weights
have to be downloaded from Hugging Face and JAX has to compile the network. Both costs are
paid once per session. The compilation is paid again for each new batch size.

## Setup cost

`preload_models` warms everything the pipeline needs, loading the three estiMINT
gradient-boosted models and both stateMINT checkpoints. It downloads them if they are not
already cached.

```{python}
import time
from estimint import preload_models

t0 = time.perf_counter()
eir_models, emulator_models = preload_models()
print(f"preload_models: {time.perf_counter() - t0:.2f} s")
print("estiMINT :", list(eir_models))
print("stateMINT:", list(emulator_models))
```

Call it once at the top of a script or a notebook. On a cold machine most of that time is
the download, roughly 38 MB per predictor. On a warm one it is deserialisation from disk.

`preload_models` tracks `main` on the model repository rather than a pinned tag. When the
exact weights matter, load the checkpoints yourself with
[`from_pretrained(..., revision=...)`](the-emulator.qmd).

## The cache

Weights land in the standard Hugging Face cache. Every later load reads from it.

```{python}
from huggingface_hub import constants

print(constants.HF_HUB_CACHE)
```

Two environment variables control this. Both must be set before the first import.

| Variable | Effect |
|---|---|
| `HF_HOME` | Relocates the whole cache. Point it at a shared or scratch filesystem on a cluster, where a home directory quota will not hold 80 MB of weights. |
| `HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1` | Forbids network access. Loads succeed from the cache and fail loudly otherwise. Set it on a compute node with no outbound route, and pre-populate the cache from the login node. |

```bash
export HF_HOME=/scratch/$USER/hf
export HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1
```

## Batching

`.predict` is a single compiled forward pass over the whole batch. The network is JIT
compiled by JAX on first use, and recompiled whenever the batch size changes. A loop of fifty
single-scenario calls performs fifty forward passes, and gets none of the parallelism the
hardware is capable of.

```{python}
import numpy as np
from stateMINT.model import Mamba2Regressor

prevalence = Mamba2Regressor.from_pretrained(
    "dide-ic/stateMINT", predictor="prevalence", revision="v1.2.2",
)

district = {
    "eir": 31.96, "dn0_use": 0.311, "dn0_future": 0.485,
    "Q0": 0.85, "phi_bednets": 0.80, "seasonal": 0,
    "routine": 0.0, "itn_use": 0.70, "irs_use": 0.0,
    "itn_future": 0.70, "irs_future": 0.0, "lsm": 0.0,
}

batch = [dict(district, eir=float(e)) for e in np.linspace(5, 60, 50)]
len(batch)
```

The first call on a given batch size pays the compilation cost. The second does not.

```{python}
t0 = time.perf_counter()
prevalence.predict(batch)
first = time.perf_counter() - t0

t0 = time.perf_counter()
prevalence.predict(batch)
second = time.perf_counter() - t0

print(f"first call  (compile + run): {first * 1000:7.0f} ms")
print(f"second call (run only)     : {second * 1000:7.0f} ms")
```

The same fifty scenarios are then run as fifty separate calls, each already compiled for a
batch of one.

```{python}
prevalence.predict([district])          # pay the batch-of-one compilation

t0 = time.perf_counter()
for scenario in batch:
    prevalence.predict([scenario])
looped = time.perf_counter() - t0

print(f"one call, 50 scenarios : {second * 1000:7.0f} ms   ({second / 50 * 1000:.1f} ms each)")
print(f"50 calls, 1 scenario   : {looped * 1000:7.0f} ms   ({looped / 50 * 1000:.1f} ms each)")
print(f"speed-up               : {looped / second:.1f}x")
```

Build the whole list of scenario dicts, then call `.predict` once. A scenario grid of a few
hundred rows is still a single call, and still under a second.

::: {.callout-note}
## Interpreting the timings

The numbers above came off whatever machine happened to run the cells. Yours will differ with
its CPU, its JAX build and whatever else it is doing. The durable part of the comparison is
the ratio between one batched call and fifty looped ones. The absolute milliseconds are not.
:::

## CPU and GPU

Those timings are CPU timings. The emulator is small, two Mamba2 layers with `d_model` 256,
and a CPU is entirely adequate at the scale of a scenario grid. There is no reason to use a
GPU to compare a dozen campaigns.

Amortised across a batch, a single scenario costs roughly **6 ms** on CPU. The same forward
pass on a GPU takes about **1 ms** (measured on an NVIDIA L40S). Either figure is several
orders of magnitude below the minutes a `malariasimulation` run of the same twelve simulated
years would take. See [Accuracy and speed](../03-concepts/validation.qmd) for the
measurements, and for what the speed costs in accuracy.

If you are running thousands of scenarios, a CUDA 12 build of JAX is available as an extra.

```bash
pip install "mintstate[gpu]"
```

Nothing in the API changes. JAX places the computation on the accelerator if it finds one, and
without a CUDA-enabled JAX installed it falls back to CPU and warns. Read that warning rather
than suppressing it. It is the only indication that the GPU is not being used.
